abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a novel coinductive framework for establishing semantic coherence in programming languages with rich type systems. Traditional approaches to coherence verification rely on syntactic techniques that fail to scale to languages featuring higher-order polymorphism, dependent types, and effect handlers. Our work introduces a semantic theory based on relational parametricity extended with greatest fixed-point operators, enabling reasoning about coherence properties as inductive invariants on infinite structures. We formalize this framework in a constructive type theory and demonstrate its applicability through three representative case studies: a calculus with gradual typing, a language supporting algebraic effects with handlers, and a dependently-typed DSL for verified compilation. The proposed framework reveals fundamental connections between coherence, type safety, and contextual equivalence that were previously unrecognized. Our results establish that the coinductive perspective not only provides greater explanatory power but also yields more elegant proofs than conventional syntactic methods. This work constitutes a paradigm shift in how researchers approach the formal verification of language designs, opening new avenues for mechanized reasoning about complex language features.

We present a significant enhancement to the classic Hindley-Milner type inference algorithm that substantially extends its expressiveness while preserving principal typing and decidability. The core limitation of traditional HM systems lies in their inability to handle polymorphic recursion combined with scoped type annotations. Our approach introduces a constrained polymorphism mechanism that allows programmers to specify polymorphic recursion boundaries through lightweight type schemes without sacrificing the algorithm's complexity guarantees. The key technical contribution is a novel constraint generation and solving strategy that operates in O(n log n) time for well-typed programs, significantly better than previous approaches requiring exponential time in pathological cases. We provide a complete formalization of the type system and inference algorithm, along with a prototype implementation demonstrating practical applicability. Experimental evaluation on real-world Haskell and ML codebases shows that our system correctly infers types for programs that were previously rejected or required substantial programmer-provided annotations. This work bridges the gap between theoretical elegance and practical utility in polymorphic type inference.

This paper introduces MetaLang, a revolutionary language workbench that unifies language design, implementation, and evolution within a single coherent framework. Existing approaches to language engineering treat syntax, semantics, and code generation as separate concerns requiring distinct tools and formalisms. MetaLang proposes a fundamentally different paradigm: a universal metalanguage where language features are first-class citizens that can be composed, inherited, and dynamically modified at runtime. Our architecture employs a novel bidirectional transformation model that guarantees consistency between abstract syntax, semantic specifications, and concrete representations. The system provides built-in support for incremental compilation, hot-swapping of language extensions, and automated generation of IDE plugins from declarative specifications. We demonstrate MetaLang's capabilities through development of three diverse DSLs: a financial contract language, a robotics control specification language, and a privacy policy DSL. Each DSL leverages the framework's composition mechanisms to share common infrastructure while maintaining domain-specific expressiveness. This work represents a paradigm shift in language-oriented programming, enabling developers to treat language engineering as an iterative, experimental process rather than a monolithic upfront design activity.

We present ModularDSL, an improved framework for constructing modular and composable domain-specific languages that addresses key limitations in existing language workbench approaches. Previous DSL construction techniques suffer from poor reusability of language modules across different domains and inability to gracefully handle feature interactions when combining extensions. ModularDSL introduces a principled module system for DSLs based on category-theoretic signatures and realizations, enabling principled composition through colimit constructions. Our framework provides a rich library of reusable language modules covering common features such as scoping, binding, data types, and control flow, along with sophisticated conflict resolution mechanisms for handling feature interactions. We developed a novel IDE infrastructure that provides domain-aware editing support even for newly composed language combinations with no hand-written tooling. The compiler backend generates efficient code through staged specialization, achieving performance competitive with hand-optimized domain-specific implementations. Evaluation across twelve DSLs from diverse application domains demonstrates that our framework reduces development effort by an average of 70% compared to traditional approaches while producing languages with superior compositionality and extensibility characteristics.
